content: Acyclovir is a medication prescribed to reduce pain and accelerate the healing of sores or blisters in individuals with varicella (chickenpox), herpes zoster (shingles, a rash that occurs in people who have previously had chickenpox), and initial or recurrent outbreaks of genital herpes (a herpes virus infection causing sores around the genital and rectal areas). It is also sometimes used to prevent genital herpes outbreaks in individuals infected with the virus. Acyclovir belongs to a class of antiviral medications known as synthetic nucleoside analogues. It works by inhibiting the spread of the herpes virus within the body. However, it does not cure genital herpes and may not prevent its transmission to others. Acyclovir is available in tablet, capsule, and liquid suspension forms for oral administration. It is typically taken with or without food two to five times daily for 5 to 10 days, starting as soon as symptoms appear. For preventing genital herpes outbreaks, it is usually taken two to five times daily for up to 12 months. It is important to take acyclovir at the same times each day and follow the prescription instructions carefully. Do not take more or less of the medication, or take it more frequently or for a longer duration than prescribed. Shake the liquid suspension well before each use to ensure even mixing. Symptoms should improve during treatment, but if they do not or worsen, contact your doctor. Complete the full course of the prescription, even if you feel better, as stopping too soon or skipping doses may result in incomplete treatment or make the infection harder to treat. Acyclovir is also used to treat eczema herpeticum (a skin infection caused by the herpes virus), to treat and prevent herpes infections of the skin, eyes, nose, and mouth in patients with HIV, and to treat oral hairy leukoplakia (a condition causing white or gray patches on the tongue or inside the cheek). It may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking acyclovir, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to acyclovir, valacyclovir (Valtrex), any other medications, or any of the ingredients in acyclovir. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. Mention specific medications such as amphotericin B, aminoglycoside antibiotics (e.g., gentamicin, tobramycin), aspirin, NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), cyclosporine, HIV medications (e.g., zidovudine), pentamidine, probenecid, sulfonamides, tacrolimus, and vancomycin, as these may interact with acyclovir. Your doctor may need to adjust doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you may be dehydrated, have immune system issues, HIV, AIDS, or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking acyclovir, contact your doctor. If you are treating genital herpes, be aware that it can still be transmitted through sexual contact even without visible symptoms and possibly even while taking acyclovir. Discuss prevention methods and whether your partner(s) should receive treatment with your doctor. While taking acyclovir, drink plenty of fluids. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, but if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Acyclovir may cause side effects. Minor side effects include upset stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, tiredness, agitation, joint pain, hair loss, and vision changes. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects include hives, rash or blisters, itching, difficulty breathing or swallowing, swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, hoarseness, fast heartbeat, weakness, pale skin, signs of infection (e.g., fever, sore throat, chills, cough), unusual bruising or bleeding, blood in urine, stomach pain or cramps, bloody diarrhea, decreased urination, headache, hallucinations, confusion, aggressive behavior, difficulty speaking, numbness or tingling in the limbs, temporary paralysis, uncontrollable shaking, seizures, or loss of consciousness. If you experience any serious side effects, contact your doctor immediately. You or your doctor may report severe side effects to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store acyclovir in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly; consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include agitation, seizures, extreme tiredness, loss of consciousness, swelling of the hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, and decreased urination. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory, as they may order tests to monitor your response to acyclovir. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist with any questions about refilling your prescription.
